_what: The talkie report's own HumanEval pass@100 series, Figure 3 (left panel).
_why_this_file_exists: The report's PROSE states no numeric pass@k anywhere. It says only that
vintage models reach non-zero pass@100, 'dramatically underperform' web-trained
models, and are 'slowly but steadily improving with scale'. The numbers below
are therefore not quoted from the text — they are the data series the figure
plots, read out of the page's own chart source. That is the primary source's
own data, not a pixel digitisation of the rendered image.

provenance.source_kind: inline client-side chart code in the report page (d3.v7)
provenance.figure_caption_verbatim: Figure 3. We gave a Python programming test (HumanEval) to a series of pairs of vintage models (trained on pre-1931 text) and modern models (trained on the web), which have the same architecture. Left: This chart shows what percentage of problems each model would get right at least once, given 100 chances and randomly chosen Python functions as examples to learn from in-context. Right: An example of a successful solution to a Python coding problem produced by a vintage language model. The model had access to several other in-context examples to learn from.
provenance.chart_title: Can a vintage model learn from examples to code?
not_found_in_source: any numeric pass@100 value in prose or in a table
the exact number of in-context demonstrations (caption says only 'several')
the number of samples n drawn per problem (pass@100 implies n >= 100)
confidence intervals or error bars of any kind

series._units: x = training FLOPs; y = HumanEval pass@100 as a fraction of 164 problems

largest_vintage_model.identification_basis: 6ND for 13B params x 260B tokens = 2.028e22 FLOPs, within 4.3% of the plotted 2.116e22; no other point on the ladder is close.
largest_vintage_model.identification_confidence: inferred, not stated in the report

matched_modern_control.identified_as: talkie-web-13b-base (same architecture, web-trained; shipped in the same HF org)
matched_modern_control.identification_confidence: inferred from the caption's 'pairs ... which have the same architecture' plus the model list in github.com/talkie-lm/talkie

caveats_on_these_numbers: 0.03215 x 164 = 5.27 problems, not an integer, so these are unbiased pass@100 estimates from n > 100 samples per problem rather than raw solve counts. The report does not state n.

The vintage series is NOT monotone: 0.014618 at 4.340e20 FLOPs drops to 0.010225 at 5.817e21. With no error bars published, the 'slowly but steadily improving' claim rests on a series that visibly reverses once. This is precisely the reason this harness refuses to report bare rates.
The report's companion chart (div#eval-charts) plots the same FLOPs ladder with three extra smaller models (1.207e17, 7.303e17, 2.838e18). Figure 3 omits those three; the report does not say why.
Demonstrations were 'randomly chosen Python functions', i.e. not curated for the target problem, and not a fixed count. A recovery curve cannot be reconstructed from a single published point.

companion_eval_series._note: From div#eval-charts on the same page. Not pass@k; included because it is the only published scale ladder for these same checkpoints and is useful for sanity-checking which point is the 13B.

worked_example_from_figure_3_right._note: The report's one displayed success. It is HumanEval/50 (decode_shift), and the model's answer differs from the in-context encode_shift by one character: + becomes -.
worked_example_from_figure_3_right.report_gloss_verbatim: All correct solutions generated by the vintage models are simple one-line programs (such as adding two inputs), or small modifications to in-context example programs.
